newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault stock hit by MAN project worries.
newsitem.headline: Renault stock hit by MAN project worries.

text.p: Shares in French carmaker Renault SA fell on Friday on a newspaper report that raised concerns about its plans to build motors jointly with Germany's MAN.
The shares were down 1.6 percent at 118 francs at 1015 GMT after recovering from an early fall of more than three percent.

Renault V.I., the truck division of Renault, and MAN have dropped plans to build a D08 motor for trucks between five and 15 tonnes, a Renault V.I. spokeswoman said on Friday, but she said the decision was not recent.
She said the two companies would pursue cooperative efforts on future motors.
"It's clearly better to start from scratch and work on a new generation," scheduled for production after the year 2000, she told Reuters.
The newspaper La Tribune Desfosses reported on Friday that the D08 deal was dead and quoted MAN officials as sounding more pessimistic about future cooperation with Renault.
It quoted MAN truck division director Rudolf Rupprecht as saying the two companies may cooperate in a future project, "but the moment hasn't come".

Renault said the D08 project was dropped mainly because of upcoming regulatory norms. "For motors between 100 and 280 horsepower, the two groups have opted to study a cooperation on entirely new motors rather than pursue common efforts based on the MAN D08 motor," it said in a statement issued in March.
But, according to the Tribune, MAN also cited delays in Renault's replacement programme and disagreement over who would have directed the project.
Traders said the article provoked the sharp fall in Renault's stock. PSA Peugeot Citroen shares and the bourse's CAC-40 index were both higher at the same time.
"Renault V.I. faces big challenges ahead," said a car analyst. "MAN has a reputation for high quality and if they're sounding negative, that would be a bit of a blow."

"The vehicle industry has to think about the concept of consolidation. Nobody's willing to grasp that at the moment," the analyst said. "Even on apparently simple collaborative ventures, it seems difficult to push ahead."
